scores.label: A
scores.note: Option 1 is 0: 'potential backlash' turns 'knows... will be angry' into a mere possibility, which changes the certainty. Option 3 is 0: 'volunteers' changes what Atticus does ('agrees' means he was asked). Options 2 and 4 hedge with 'probable', 2 is stiff ('cognizant'), and 5 drops 'most', so all three are only usable.

scores.label: B
scores.note: Option 2 is 0: 'volunteers' changes 'agrees', so it changes what happens. Option 5 is 0: 'potential for public backlash' hedges a known outcome and drops 'most'. Option 1 adds 'willingly', and option 3 is in the passive and hedges with 'likely'. Option 4 is the best one, but it sits fourth.

scores.label: C
scores.note: Option 3 is 0: 'willing to support' loses the legal sense of 'defend', and 'upset' is not more academic. Option 5 is 0: 'many' replaces 'most', 'act on behalf of' is vague, and 'angry about it' is casual. Option 1 ('is prepared to') drifts from 'agrees' and drops 'most'. Option 4 hedges with 'likely' and turns anger into 'oppose his position'.

scores.label: D
scores.note: Option 1 is 0: it drops 'knows', adds the hedge 'likely' and changes 'most' to 'many'. Option 2 is 0: it is almost a copy of the original with only will->would, so the register does not change. Option 5 is 0: it presents the anger as already there instead of foreseen, drops 'knows', and 'widespread anger of most' is redundant. Option 3 is plain and drops 'he knows' but is still usable. Option 4 failed as a duplicate and was not judged.

scores.label: E
scores.note: All five keep the knowledge, the 'most/majority' and the certain 'will'. Option 2 is a little stiff ('harbor anger'). Option 5 is plainer ('angry at him') and loses the concessive link. The sentences are built alike, so variety is moderate.
